one_liner: Rust auto-growing cuckoo filter, a retuned copy of sile/scalable_cuckoo_filter; 4-5.6x faster positive lookups than it and cuckoofilter.
what_it_does: It is an approximate-membership set with deletion that grows on its own. When an insert fails after max_kicks (default 512) evictions, it adds a new cuckoo filter layer with twice the capacity and half the false-positive budget, in the style of scalable Bloom filters. The API is `CuckooFilter<T, H>::new(capacity_hint, fpp)` or a builder, with `add_if_not_exist`, `add` (no duplicate check), `contains`, `remove`, `shrink_to_fit`, `*_hash` variants for precomputed u64 hashes, and `contains_batch`. It is not a drop-in for the upstream crate: method names differ, there is no RNG type parameter, and serialization uses bitcode instead of serde.
how_it_is_fast: It keeps the upstream's partial-key cuckoo hashing (Fan et al., CoNEXT'14) with bit-packed fingerprints and 4-entry buckets. When a bucket fits in 64 bits it is read with a single unaligned 128-bit load and all slots are compared branchlessly with `|`, where the upstream reads each slot in a bounds-checked byte loop; inserts find the matching and empty slots in the same pass. The alternate bucket index, which costs a second hash of the fingerprint, is computed only when the first bucket misses, while the upstream always computes it. The default hasher is gxhash (AES-NI/NEON) instead of the upstream's SipHash-1-3.
when_to_use: A Rust service needs a 'definitely absent' pre-check with deletions for a key set that grows without a known final size, for example in front of an index or WAL write path, as the README's example shows.
String or byte-slice keys (the bench used random 8-128 byte keys) on hardware with AES instructions, where hashing dominates the cost of a lookup.
Lookups that are mostly for keys that are present. The deferred second hash pays off most there, because most positive lookups hit the first bucket.
You already use sile's scalable_cuckoo_filter and want the same layout and memory footprint (both 353 KB in the bench) with faster operations, and you can rename a few calls.
Servers or Apple Silicon builds where you control RUSTFLAGS (e.g. -C target-cpu=native).
when_not_to_use: Portable x86-64 binaries built without extra RUSTFLAGS. The default gxhash feature does not compile there, and turning it off falls back to std's SipHash, which voids the published numbers.

Static or rarely changing sets. In the bench it used about 29 bits per key (353 KB for 100k keys at 0.17% measured FPP, because bucket counts round up to a power of two and the filter was 38% full), and immutable xor/binary-fuse filters are far smaller.
Workloads dominated by keys that are absent. These were never benchmarked; every miss hashes twice and probes both buckets in every layer, so the cost grows with the number of growth layers.
Concurrent writers. There is no concurrent API: mutation takes &mut self, so you need an external lock or sharding.

Projects that are strict about maturity or licensing: 3 stars, about 1.1k downloads, MulanPSL-2.0 declared only in Cargo.toml and the README with no LICENSE file, and the upstream's MIT notice is not reproduced.

integration.dependencies: fastrand, bitcode (derive); gxhash by default (optional); museair optional
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2024 edition (rustc 1.85+); no rust-version declared; benchmarked on rustc 1.98.0
integration.platforms: Default gxhash feature: x86/x86-64 with aes+sse2 or ARM with aes+neon enabled at compile time; a stock x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu build fails. Built out of the box on Apple M2 Max (the author's bench machine). With default-features = false or museair it should build anywhere Rust std does (not tested).
integration.thread_safety: not documented; plain struct with &self lookups and &mut self mutations, no internal synchronization
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same algorithm and memory layout as sile's scalable_cuckoo_filter, but insert_if_not_contained/insert become add_if_not_exist/add, there is no RNG parameter, and serde is replaced by bitcode; the API is unrelated to the cuckoofilter crate's add/test_and_add/delete

gotchas: `cargo add autoscale_cuckoo_filter` does not build on default x86-64 targets. gxhash 3.5 raises compile_error! unless aes+sse2 are enabled, and docs.rs builds of 0.5.26 and 0.5.27 failed for this reason, so recent versions have no hosted docs. Set RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" (or +aes,+sse2) or use default-features = false.

The README is wrong about the hasher and serialization. It says the default hasher is RapidHash and advertises optional serde, but the code uses gxhash::GxHasher (std SipHash with no hash feature) and supports bitcode only. The hasher field is skipped when encoding, so a filter built with a custom or seeded hasher decodes with H::default() and returns wrong answers. The gxhash docs also say hashes may change across its major versions and warn that the unseeded default hasher is open to DoS.

The branchless one-load bucket path only applies while fingerprint bits x entries <= 64 (16-bit fingerprints at 4 entries). Each growth layer adds one fingerprint bit, so an FPP below about 2.4e-4, or a fourth layer at the default 0.001, falls back to a per-entry loop.

The usual cuckoo deletion hazards apply, and the README documents them at length. `add` stores duplicates. Removing a key that was never inserted can delete a colliding fingerprint and cause a false negative. `len()` is approximate.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over xorf (static xor/binary fuse, smaller and faster but immutable) or fastbloom (no deletion) when a Rust set must take inserts and deletes and grow without a known size. The C++ efficient/cuckoofilter reference and CGCL's Dynamic Cuckoo Filter cover the same ground outside Rust, and no head-to-head numbers against them exist.
verified_claims_summary: The author benchmarked on an Apple M2 Max (macOS 26.5.1, rustc 1.98.0, opt-level 3, mimalloc) with one Instant-timed pass over 100k random 8-128 byte keys in a filter sized for 200k (about 38% full). Positive lookups ran at 81.0 M/s vs 14.6 M/s for sile's scalable_cuckoo_filter 0.5.1 (SipHash-1-3) and 20.4 M/s for cuckoofilter 0.5 (FarmHasher, given 10x capacity). Adds ran at 21.8 vs 9.1/14.9 M/s and removes at 53.5 vs 13.6/13.5 M/s. The contenders use different hash functions, so part of the gap comes from the hasher rather than the filter. The README's '4.5x/3x' headline comes from an older table that gives no environment.
status_note: Actively released (19 crates.io versions from 2025-12-29 to 0.5.27 on 2026-09-06), but it is a 3-star monorepo crate whose per-crate CI file sits in a subdirectory that GitHub Actions does not run. It is about 2,000 lines of Rust including tests, so it is easy to vendor under MulanPSL-2.0 once the gxhash build flags are handled.
